stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

stories.headline: Broncos offense searching for more big plays, ready for Bo Nix to 'let it rip'
stories.summary: Changing playcallers wasn't an immediate fix for the Broncos' offense, which still suffers from a lack of big plays and a QB who hasn't found his rhythm.
stories.body:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. -- In the moments following a tooth-grinding escape against the winless Los Angeles Chargers, Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton talked about his continued wrestling match with time.

The Broncos hope to slightly slow quarterback Bo Nix's internal clock between the snap and the whistle to end each play. And they feel like succeeding with that adjustment would cause everything to fall into place for Nix and the Denver offense so they can, in Payton's words, "let it rip."

"There's a lot that's been said about his feet, I think he's settling that down," Payton said in the moments after Sunday's 23-17 victory over the 0-5 Chargers. "[But] I think it's important from a protection standpoint we provide that early in game so that clock doesn't get juiced up a little bit."

The Broncos moved to 3-2 with the victory, but it was not a smooth operation for the offense in its first game since Payton re-assumed playcalling duties. Denver finished 1-of-12 on third down against the Chargers, gained only 224 net yards and had one play longer than 12 yards before the fourth quarter. Nix finished with the second-lowest passing yardage of his career (16-of-27 passing for 123 yards and a touchdown).

Following Sunday's games, Nix is 24th in the league in QBR (43.1) and 30th in completion percentage over expectation (minus-4.1%), ahead of only Cleveland's Deshaun Watson. The Broncos find themselves near the bottom of the league in most statistical categories on offense, including scoring (29th, 18.0 points per game). Only the Arizona Cardinals have fewer plays of 20 yards or more than the Broncos' 11.

These struggles are part of why Payton snatched playcalling duties back from offensive coordinator Davis Webb after four games. But Payton's playcalling return saw many of the same issues that prompted him to make the change. And a coach who has made his résumé on a brash, go-for-it boldness spoke of the benefit of "small steps" for the QB as the Broncos' defense once again fueled a fourth-quarter comeback win.

"Thought guys up front settled in," Payton said. "... And when we needed it, [Nix] gave us some important ones."

Much of the outside angst about Denver's offense has centered on the 26-year-old quarterback's play. Many former QBs, including ESPN analyst Chase Daniel, who played for Payton in New Orleans, have spoken of Nix's footwork and his penchant for moving through his progressions too quickly before Broncos receivers are into their routes enough to be targets.

Payton has acknowledged some of that, saying that he wants "make [Nix's] job easier" with a better run-game approach and improved pass protection, especially early in games, to get the QB settled faster. That mindset was apparent Sunday, which was the first game this season in which the Broncos had more rushing attempts than pass attempts.

Though the Broncos rushed for fewer than 4 yards per carry on their 29 attempts (106 yards for 3.7 per carry), Payton said he believes the rhythm of the run game is important in helping Nix play with a little more freedom. Nix, who had two ankle surgeries this past offseason, has run less this season, and his 5.7 air yards per attempt currently ranks last among the league's 31 qualifying quarterbacks.

"I think after [five] weeks there's a handful of things collectively, it starts with me, where it's like 'alright, where it's let's focus on the details' and I think the by-product helps the [quarterback]," Payton said. "I think the hardest thing to do in this league is play that position if you're not rushing the ball."

Payton said he and the Broncos coaches have assured Nix that he's "the guy we want here." Nix has also acknowledged that he has tried to not press when things aren't going smoothly and that he, too, wants to find the let-it-rip zone.

"When a coach says 'let it rip,' it means play what you see, have good vision, and I think there's just, right now, there's just a little subtle piece that's overall offensive execution that we're still working toward," Nix said. "Because at times it's there and at times, for whatever reason, the drive stalls."

When the Broncos selected Nix with the 12th overall pick in 2024, Payton said it was in large part due to Nix's "superpower" -- his ability to avoid sacks and turnovers. But Nix has fumbled four times this season, including twice on Sunday, one which he lost. Nix knows he must be more careful before truly being able to let loose.

"Letting it rip is one of the best things that you can do as a quarterback," Nix said. "At the same time, you've got to sort of earn that right. When you do the preparation, you earn the right to react so that you can let it rip."

Things don't get any easier this week. The Broncos have a short week before a Thursday night game against the 3-2 Seattle Seahawks, the defending Super Bowl champions. Seattle is ninth in scoring defense and has surrendered the fewest yards per play in the NFL (4.2). The Seahawks are also tied for fourth in the league in quick pressures, which will challenge Nix's ability to slow down his internal clock.

"[Hall of Fame coach] Bill [Parcells] taught me one thing and it's on going, if you're not having the output you're looking for, you have to look at reducing the variables," Payton said. "And we're trying to do that, reduce the variables so guys can play faster."

stories.headline: When can Kimi Antonelli win the F1 title? Earliest date, points needed and remaining races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Max Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant drive at Singapore GP

- Lewis Hamilton calls Singapore GP strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: Olivier Giroud on leaving Arsenal: 'Toughest' decision of my career
stories.summary: Oliver Giroud said leaving Arsenal was the "toughest choice" of his career as he prepares to make his Emirates Stadium comeback, aged 40.
stories.body:
Olivier Giroud said leaving Arsenal was the "toughest choice" of his career as he prepares to make his Emirates Stadium comeback, aged 40.

Giroud scored 105 times in 235 appearances across nearly six years for Arsene Wenger's Gunners before leaving to join Chelsea ahead of the 2018 World Cup.

The former France international departed Stamford Bridge for AC Milan before a one-year stint in Major League Soccer for Los Angeles FC.

However, Giroud returned to his homeland last year and the striker is set to face his one-time employers when Lille face Arsenal in north London on Tuesday night.

"Arsenal was a major part of my career and I had to leave in order to play at the 2018 World Cup," Giroud said.

"I was really sad when I left the club but I had to make that choice, and it was one of the toughest ones in my career, but it was important and necessary for the rest of my career.

"So, it is great to come back at 40 years old with a French club and to play against Mikel Arteta's Arsenal. That is a blessing. It is something I wanted to happen, and I feel very lucky."

Giroud was a three-time FA Cup winner at Arsenal but failed to land the Premier League during his time with the club.

- Arsenal's Gabriel ready to take another penalty despite Champions League final miss

- Arsenal's Jurriën Timber 'happy' with Ben White competition at right-back

He played alongside Arteta and said the 44-year-old Spaniard, who has recently signed a new contract to remain at the Emirates until 2030, was always destined for management.

Arteta last season led the Gunners to their first league title in 22 years.

Giroud continued: "Mikel is a great person, a great manager and he has shown that with the team he has built.

"The Premier League title proves he has done incredible work, and he was given the time which was very important.

"I remember Mikel as a player, and you could see he was made for a managerial career because he was a leader on the pitch, but off it, too. He was very demanding with himself, and his team-mates and great technically.

"I really enjoyed my time with him. We won a few trophies together and it is a blessing to come back here and play against his team."

stories.headline: Man United could never contend for the Premier League title -- but they aren't so bad either
stories.summary: Man United fans go from thinking the team will win the Premier League to thinking the sky is falling. The truth is in the middle and it's unlikely to shift.
stories.body:
If you've followed Manchester United for the past 10 years or so, you know the story by now. It goes something like this.

First, there's a bad season. The richest team in the Premier League somehow finishes too low to qualify for the Champions League. A previously beloved manager suddenly looks clueless. A bunch of highly paid, previously successful players barely look good enough to play in the Premier League, let alone for a team that wants to compete for every major trophy.

Inevitably, the manager is fired -- either before the season ends, over the summer, or just a couple of weeks into the new season. Then, a new guy comes in, the results get better, a lot of those inept players suddenly look capable, and the team finishes way above where it landed under the previous guy.

The team qualifies for the Champions League, then it spends a ton of money on a bunch of players, and the whispers begin: I kind of think United could win the league. And then the whispers turn into shouts, given so many of England's former-players-turned-pundits used to play for the club.

Inevitably, the cycle then restarts anew. Not only does the club fail to meet the unrealistic expectations but doesn't even come close. Everyone turns on the coach they said was a savior six months ago. All of those new players who were going to push them to their first title since 2013 struggle to even keep them afloat.

The coach gets fired, they hire someone new, the results improve, a title is suddenly on the cards, and then it all falls apart -- again and again.

And again: like, right now. After finishing third last season, Man United have earned only six points from their first six matches. This past weekend's draw against 10-man Tottenham condemned the club to their worst league start since 1986.

The club looks as if it's going to get lost in its vicious cycle once again -- but how might United, uh, not do that?

First, they'd need to figure out how to create realistic expectations for the immediate future -- unadorned and uncomplicated by what all the fans and former players want the club to be. And then they'd need to find a new way to assess team performance beyond what the table says.

If there's any club that should be aware that past point totals don't predict future point totals, it's the one that has finished sixth, third, eighth, 15th and third over the past three years.

And once Man United figured out how to do both of those things? Everyone at the club might realize that things aren't that far off from what they should've expected.

Why Man United haven't been title contenders and fans should stop expecting it
Analyzing Manchester United used to be pretty simple. This was one of the three richest clubs in the world, and this club was consistently not even finishing inside the top three of its own domestic league. A robot, a child using video-game ratings from FIFA, a random fan, even Gary Neville -- they could all have produced similar results from that massive resource advantage.

But despite the efforts of various American owners to build new stadiums, create "matchday experiences," raise ticket prices, and convince English fans that they need an All-Star game, there is still only one tried-and-true way of increasing revenues.

OK fine, there are two, and I'll quickly address the $1 billion elephant in the room. One way you can boost your revenue is by implementing, as the Premier League put it, "sham contracts" and "sham agreements" ... "to artificially inflate [your] club's revenues." What Manchester City did to cheat the rules and what the Premier League is going to do about it will, unfortunately, be hanging over everything you're about to read and everything we're going to watch this season.

But beyond the Man City method, there's one main way to make your soccer club richer: win more soccer games.

You win more prize money by finishing higher in the table. You give your club the kind of advertising no billboard can match. You qualify for European tournaments, like the Champions League, which earn you extra broadcast revenue and matchday revenue.

We've slowly seen this all play out at Old Trafford -- in the opposite direction. As Manchester United's performance level has steadily dropped over time, so too have the club's revenues.

For the 24 seasons from 1996-97 to 2019-20, United never ranked lower than fourth, globally, in annual revenue. And in most years, they were significantly higher than that. Over those 24 seasons, United recorded the highest revenues of any club 10 times -- bested only by Real Madrid's 12. Barcelona were the only other club to nab the top spot: twice.

But since 2019-20, United haven't landed higher than fourth, and they've fallen outside of the top four three times: fifth twice and then, in the most recent accounting year, eighth.

This chart shows the revenue rankings of the so-called Big Six since 2003-04, when Manchester City broke into Deloitte's annual Money League ranking:

That massive upward spike from the bottom, of course, is the 10-year period for which Man City were just found guilty. But with Man United, you can see that they were the highest-ranked Premier League club until 2019-20. If in 2010, you told the owners of Liverpool and Arsenal that their clubs would eventually make more money than Manchester United, they would've laughed in your face. Well, in 2024-25, they both did.

Another way to look at this is to see just how high United's floor is. In the 2024-25 season, they literally finished in 17th place. Despite that, they still brought in top-10 revenues globally. This goes a long way to explaining the on-field volatility over the past 10 years: The club has been managed terribly, so they have bad seasons, but they also have so much money that they also have a couple of decent seasons.

The main takeaway, though, is that United are no longer the standalone richest Premier League club. They are one of the richest Premier League clubs. On top of that, they've come back to the super-club pack right when the rest of the Premier League -- the other 14 teams -- have ascended to a new level.

The players who don't sign with a top-10 team in the world are no longer joining AC Milan or Borussia Dortmund -- no, they're going to Aston Villa and Nottingham Forest. So, not only do United no longer have a built-in revenue advantage over their closest competitors, the rest of the league has also seen its talent level rise.

What should United's expectations be, then? Per the site Transfermarkt, they have the fifth-most valuable squad in the Premier League. Per the estimates from the site FBref, they have the fourth-highest wage bill. And per the most recent accounting, they have the fourth-highest revenues.

Given all of that, their baseline expectation at the current moment should be around fourth or fifth place in the Premier League.

Why Man United are better than they seem right now -- and whether it matters
Manchester United, of course, are currently in 13th place. But we know that there's a lot of noise over the first six matches of the season. Or, at least, we know that the Premier League table after six games isn't a great predictor of what the Premier League table will look like after 38 games.

Take last season: Liverpool had a three-point lead atop the table, and Tottenham were in fourth. Over the next year, the clubs combined to fire three different managers and neither team finished anywhere near where they were through six games.

If we just look at goals scored and conceded, it already looks a tiny bit better for United: tied for the ninth-best mark in the league with Liverpool. Granted, a neutral goal differential still isn't great for either of those clubs, but it's at least better than where United currently sit in the table.

If we take it a step further and look at all of the shots every team in the league has conceded -- close to 1,200 so far this season -- instead of just the 170-plus that have crossed the goal line, then things improve even more.

Through six games, Man United have the league's sixth-best expected goal (xG) differential -- from the fifth-most xG created and the seventh-fewest xG conceded. Through Michael Carrick's first 17 matches as head coach in charge last season? United had the fifth-best xG differential -- from the sixth-most xG created and the fourth-fewest xG conceded.

Though the performances have been a bit worse -- against one of the easiest schedules in the league -- the biggest reason, by far, for why the vibes have shifted so suddenly is the mostly random nature of what happens once a player's foot or head comes into contact with the ball. A team with the fifth-ish most talented team in the league is playing like the sixth-ish best team in the league, and the variance of finishing chances has pushed United down the table.

This is not to say that United have been great or anything like that. They really struggled against Tottenham before they went up a man, and in the previous match against Man City, they really struggled even after they went up a man.

Based on how United are playing, there are reasons to be optimistic and pessimistic -- at the same time.

They have attempted 17 more shots (125) than any team in the league, and they're only one behind (65) Arsenal and Bournemouth for fewest conceded. They have taken 64% of the final-third touches in their matches -- most in the league. And they've taken 62.4% of the penalty-area touches in their matches -- second only to Manchester City.

Teams that dominate all of those areas of play tend to finish near the top of the table -- not with neutral goal differentials and down near the bottom half.

At the same time, United do frequently look like a team that wants to dominate the ball but without a real plan for what to do with it -- or for what happens when they lose it.

Per Gradient Sports, United lead the league in both the number and percentage of shots attempted with a better passing option available. They're crossing the ball more often than any team in the league. And despite dominating territory, they sit in the middle of the pack for just about every pressing metric. That suggests that their opponents are happy to let them have the ball.

United know what to do but not how to do it -- something you might expect from a team coached by someone with no top-level experience.

But this also was all true under Carrick last season. We knew United were boosted by being eliminated from both cup competitions early in the season and by not qualifying for Europe. Now, after the disappointing draw with Tottenham, they have to fly to Spain and go play Diego Simeone's Atletico Madrid. Last season, they would've had a full week to regroup.

Not only that, but now Carrick has to deal with the kind of situation that separates top coaches from average, replaceable ones: figuring out whether something needs to change or whether something will change as long as you convince your players that you actually don't need to change anything.

If you took a step back and tried to analyze last season objectively, there wasn't a particularly strong argument for hiring or replacing Carrick. United kept him, and then the same thing happened that always happens.

If they decide to move on from Carrick, then we can all probably guess what might come next: things will get better, then they'll get worse. And in another year or two, we'll get to do it all over again.

stories.headline: Source: Dodgers' decision on sitting Ohtani hinges on health
stories.summary: The Dodgers will gauge whether Shohei Ohtani's lingering injuries warrant him sitting out but will keep playing him if he deems himself healthy, a source said.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- The Los Angeles Dodgers plan to gauge whether superstar Shohei Ohtani's lingering injuries warrant him sitting out Game 3 of the National League Championship Series but will continue playing him if he deems himself healthy, a source told ESPN.

Ohtani went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts in a 7-4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 on Monday that put the Dodgers in a 2-0 hole in the best-of-seven series. Afterward, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told The Athletic he would have "a conversation" with Ohtani during Tuesday's workout in L.A. to "try to figure out what's best for him."

But a source clarified that the team would sit Ohtani only if he believed he was compromised by the left knee and right bicep injuries that previously hindered him. If he feels good enough to play, the plan is to continue playing him.

Ohtani has not homered since Aug. 18 and has produced only three hits in 20 postseason at-bats. Over the past eight weeks, a stretch in which he went on the injured list in hopes of helping his body recover, he is slashing .156/.283/.200.

"It's hard to see," Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts said of Ohtani's struggles. "He's working, and hopefully he gets out of it. We know he's working. Yeah, that's a big one. We need him for sure."

When Betts grounded out for the first out of the fifth inning Monday, he pumped his fist in celebration. To him, it meant something more -- that Tommy Edman would move to third base, allowing him to later score the go-ahead run on a sacrifice fly, and that perhaps the Dodgers had finally tapped into something against this vaunted Brewers pitching staff.

Betts' zeal, it turns out, was fleeting.

For the second time in as many games in this NLCS, the Dodgers were shut down by a dominant bullpen in the later innings, unable to match a relentless Brewers offense that continuously applied pressure. Rather than set the tone, Betts' groundout represented the first of 15 consecutive outs recorded by Brewers relievers, a sign that the Dodgers' struggles extend well beyond Ohtani.

Thirty-six of the past 38 teams that faced a 2-0 deficit in a best-of-seven series were ultimately eliminated. To Freddie Freeman and so many of his teammates, the reason the Dodgers are in this position is quite simple.

"They got on base and got the hits," Freeman said. "It's hard to win games when you only get three hits."

Once again, none of those hits came with runners in scoring position. The Dodgers went 0-for-4 in that situation in Game 2 and are now 2-for-26 with runners in scoring position in these playoffs, with both of those hits coming off the bat of Andy Pages. Of the 19 runs the Dodgers have scored in their first six games this month, 11 have come via home run.

The struggles are collective, but none feel bigger than the ones endured by Ohtani.

The most glaring sign of his struggles occurred in Monday's sixth inning, when he squared to bunt to begin his at-bat. Five JoJo Romero pitches later, he struck out while awkwardly chasing a sweeper well out of the zone.

"It's tough," Dodgers outfielder Teoscar Hernandez said. "We obviously need his help. He's a big, big part of this team, and it's really important. And just like, you know, I feel bad for him. I know what he's capable of. He's been dealing with some stuff in the past. We don't know if it's still there. But it's Shohei. Any moment, he can come through."

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, arguably the best postseason pitcher going right now, was removed after recording only eight outs and throwing 75 pitches -- 12 of them in one encounter with Jake Bauers, who drew a third-inning walk to load the bases and set up Christian Yelich's two-run single, forcing Roberts to go to his bullpen earlier than he had hoped.

If Will Smith challenges two borderline two-strike pitches to Brice Turang in the first and third innings, both of which ultimately led to runs, maybe Yamamoto's outing looks different. If Roberts brings Roki Sasaki back out for the fifth inning -- rather than turning to lefty Kris Bubic, who proceeded to give up the William Contreras home run that tied the score at 4 -- maybe the Brewers don't gain momentum. And if Brock Stewart doesn't make an errant pickoff throw to first base in the bottom of the sixth, allowing David Hamilton to later score on Contreras' single, maybe everything is different.

But the reality is this: The Dodgers' offense has produced almost nothing late.

In Game 1, they stressed Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski enough to force him out in the fifth inning. In Game 2, they did the same to rookie Logan Henderson, who was removed after his second throwing error. But in both, six relievers -- a group headlined by Aaron Ashby, Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill -- combined to allow only five of 33 batters to reach to reach base.

The last time the Dodgers dropped the first two games in a playoff series, it was 2023. They were swept out of the NL Division Series by a red-hot Arizona Diamondbacks team then. Immediately after that, they signed Ohtani, surrounded him with a host of high-priced stars and won the next two championships.

Now the question is whether Ohtani will be there to help them get out of this hole.

"We're all still behind him," Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. "He knows we're all still behind him. He's going to get a big hit for us. I know that. I can tell you right now he's going to get a big hit for us at some point, and that's going to turn things."

stories.headline: Ranking every AFL free agent by the impact they'll have at their new club
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL free agency period is now complete. We've ranked every move that has been made, factoring in positional needs and their likely impact for season 2027.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL free agency period is now complete, with seven players finding new clubs either as restricted or unrestricted free agents.

We've ranked every move that has been made, factoring in positional needs and their likely impact for season 2027 (not the rest of their career). So, who will be the biggest needle mover of the bunch in the immediate future?

7. Kieren Briggs
This is absolutely no criticism of Kieren Briggs, but there really aren't many players in the competition (if any) that could be dropped into the Tigers in 2027 and be serious needle movers. Remember, Richmond has won just 10 games across the last three seasons and is widely expected to finish in the bottom four once again next year. Tigers skipper Toby Nankervis will remain the club's primary ruck in the immediate future, but the arrival of Briggs will allow for a new-look one-two punch. The former Giant is one of the best hitout-to-advantage rucks in the game and an elite clearance winner. At 27 years of age, and with Nankervis now 32, Briggs' impact will likely be felt in the years beyond 2027.

6. Jordon Butts
Key defensive stocks have been a concern for the Bulldogs in recent years, so the signing of Jordon Butts will be a welcomed addition for the club. Butts makes the move after eight seasons and 94 games with the Crows, but he's managed just 10 and nine games in 2025 and 2026. Throughout different parts of the last couple of years, he's struggled with unlucky injuries; in 2025 it was a collapsed lung, and this year he battled concussion and a fractured foot. With the continued strong form of Josh Worrell and Mark Keane, and emergence of Josh Borlase at the Crows, a move to the Bulldogs makes sense for both the 26-year-old Butts and the Dogs.

5. Joel Amartey
The Blues landed key forward support for Harry McKay in the form of Joel Amartey, who crosses from the Swans as an unrestricted free agent. It's a shrewd acquisition for Carlton, and the club will be hopeful he can be an upgrade on both Brodie Kemp and Mitch McGovern. Amartey is coming off a season at Sydney in which he booted 28 goals from 15 games and averaged three marks per game. In 2024 he enjoyed a career-best 43-goal campaign, including a bag of nine against the Crows. Amartey is just 27 years of age and should only really be coming into his prime as a key position player in the AFL. Could surprise a few in 2027.

4. Toby Greene
Another year, another major coup for the Cats. Is anyone surprised?! Former Giants captain Toby Greene joins Geelong as an unrestricted free agent while GWS has to make do with second-round compensation. We all know Greene has been a high-impact player throughout his 15-year career and he will add a whole new dynamic to the Cats' forward line, one that features former Giants teammate and close friend Jeremy Cameron. In 2026, Greene kicked 34 goals -- his lowest return in a season since his injury-interrupted 2020 campaign -- but did amass over 20 disposals per game. If anyone wanted to argue he deserves the top spot on this list I wouldn't scoff, but it's not as if the Cats had trouble scoring in 2026...

3. Ben King
It may have been a move that surprised few, but it's one -- along with the signing of Zach Merrett, of course -- that will have Hawks fans believing a premiership is possible in 2027. For a fair chunk of the 2026 season, King looked to be the Coleman Medal winner. Gold Coast's capitulation didn't help his chances, though he still finished the home and away season with 60 goals to his name -- the third consecutive year he's managed 55+ goals. King will partner veteran Jack Gunston and dynamo Nick Watson in what now looks to be one of the most dangerous forward lines in the game.

2. Lachie Neale
The Lachie Neale-Brisbane Lions era is over, with the two-time Brownlow Medal winner joining Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent and partnering reigning Brownlow winner Nick Daicos in a new-look Magpies midfield. Neale might be 33 years of age and on the downturn of his decorated career, but he still averaged 29 disposals, 12.5 contested possessions, and six clearances per outing in 2026 and figures to be a major contributor next season in a Collingwood engine room that's often lacked depth and firepower. Even if the Magpies receive 80-85% of this season's production from Neale, he'll be difficult to top as the most impactful free agent of the year.

1. Zak Butters
The most sought after man in football made the decision to sign with the Bulldogs during free agency. Former Power star Zak Butters joins the club as a top five player in the game, and at age 26, you can certainly make the argument he's only at the beginning of his prime. Butters will partner Western Bulldogs skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in what's easily the most impressive and dynamic three-pronged midfield in the competition. He offers a real point of difference, too, with his electric pace and the ability to break lines two eye-catching features that have seen him ascend to footy superstardom.

stories.headline: St. Louis unbeaten run up to 20 games, tying Red Bulls' MLS record
stories.summary: Carlo Holse's hat trick helped St. Louis City SC beat the LA Galaxy 6-2 on Sunday night to extend their unbeaten streak across all competitions to 20 games.
stories.body:
ST. LOUIS -- Carlo Holse's hat trick in the first 21 minutes -- the second hat trick in club history -- helped St. Louis City beat the LA Galaxy 6-2 on Sunday night to extend their unbeaten streak across all competitions to 20 games and tie the MLS record.

St. Louis, which is 13-0-5 in its last 18 regular-season games, tied the mark set when the New York Red Bulls went unbeaten in an MLS-record 20 consecutive games across all competitions in 2016.

Rafael Navarro converted from the penalty spot in the 45th minute, scored again in the 53rd and added two assists for St. Louis (14-6-8). Lukas MacNaughton scored on a diving header in the seventh minute of first-half stoppage time and Roman Bürki had five saves.

Holse opened the scoring in the second minute, added a goal in the seventh and skipped a shot inside the right post from the center of the area to make it 3-0 in the 21st minute to record the second-fastest hat trick in MLS history. Hany Mukhtar scored three goals for Nashville in the first 16 minutes of 5-1 win over Chicago on July 17, 2021.

The Galaxy's Kyōgo Furuhashi went off due to an apparent hamstring injury and was replaced in the 10th minute by João Klauss, whose goal in the 71st minute capped the scoring. Klauss, a 29-year-old midfielder in his first season with the Galaxy, had St. Louis City's first hat trick in a 3-3 tie with the Galaxy on June 14, 2025.

Robert Taylor scored in the 31st minute for the Galaxy (9-11-9).

St. Louis beat the Galaxy 3-1 on July 22 at Dignity Health Sports Park and hosts the Vancouver Whitecaps on Wednesday in a Western Conference top-of-table clash.

The Galaxy, who are clinging to the last playoff spot in the West, play the Portland Timbers at Dignity Health Sports Park on Wednesday. The Timbers are three points behind the Galaxy for ninth place -- the final playoff spot.

stories.headline: Location of Dream home games for WNBA Finals still uncertain
stories.summary: The Dream, dealing with conflicting events at State Farm Arena, are still determining where they will play their home games during the upcoming WNBA Finals.
stories.body:
The location of the Atlanta Dream's home games for the WNBA Finals had not been determined as of Sunday night.

The Dream, who will face the Golden State Valkyries in the best-of-seven series, are scheduled to host Games 3, 4 and 6 (if necessary) on Oct. 22, 24 and 29. The Dream's home arena since 2021 has been Gateway Center Arena at College Park, which holds only 3,500 fans. That small capacity is a concern for the Finals, but at this point, the Dream have not said if they have secured a larger facility.

Dream president and chief operating officer Morgan Shaw Parker, speaking to the media last week, said the team was "finalizing details on their home venue and where we will be playing" for the Finals. The Dream and the WNBA did not offer further details Sunday when contacted by ESPN.

The Valkyries will host Games 1, 2, and also 5 and 7 (if necessary) at their home, the Chase Center in San Francisco, which has a capacity of 18,064.

This year, the Dream moved six regular-season home games and all three of their previous home playoff games to State Farm Arena in downtown Atlanta -- which will also be the team's full-time home next season. The capacity there is 17,044. But State Farm is booked with a Sombr concert on Oct. 22 and Atlanta Hawks regular-season games on Oct. 24 and 29.

The Dream previously were based at State Farm (then known as Philips Arena) from the franchise's inception in 2008 to 2016. Refurbishments at the arena led to the Dream playing at Georgia Tech's McCamish Pavilion in 2017-2018. The arena's name was changed to State Farm in 2019, and the Dream returned there for that season. Then the Dream relocated to the much smaller Gateway Center in 2021.

But the WNBA's and the Dream's increased popularity have prompted the move back to State Farm starting in 2027. The Washington Mystics played three games of the 2019 WNBA Finals at their home, CareFirst Arena, which seats 4,200. That was the last time the WNBA Finals were played at a venue that had fewer than 8,000 seats except 2020, when the entire WNBA season was played in a COVID-19 bubble facility without fans in Bradenton, Florida.

Several playoff games in the past, including in the WNBA Finals, have been played in alternate venues during the league's 30-season history because of facility conflicts or renovations. The Dream hosted a 2013 WNBA Finals game at the Arena at Gwinnett Center in Duluth, Georgia. That facility is now known as Gas South Arena and seats around 13,000.

There also have been WNBA Finals games played at college arenas such as Eastern Michigan (2008), University of Illinois Chicago (2014), USC (2016), Minnesota (2017) and George Mason (2018).

stories.headline: New Zealand Rugby launches legal action against ARLC over 'Chiefs' name
stories.summary: The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.
stories.body:
The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.

NZR on Thursday said it had been left with no choice but to launch legal proceedings against the ARLC, who has sought to adopt the name for its Papua New Guinea expansion franchise.

The PNG Chiefs are due to join the NRL in 2028 and have already signed a raft of players, including code-hoppers Zac Lomaz and Joey Manu, but they may yet have to undergo a chanGe of name if NZR gets its way.

The Chiefs' Super Rugby franchise has existed since 1996, with NZR claiming the introduction of the PNG Chiefs would result in "significant confusion and damage" should they be allowed to compete under the name from 2028.

"New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has today moved to protect the Chiefs brand and is filing proceedings in the High Court of New Zealand against the decision by the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) to launch a new NRL side using "Chiefs" in its name," an NZR statement read.  

"NZR is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names 'PNG Chiefs', 'Chiefs' or any other similar names in New Zealand.   

"The Chiefs have competed as a professional rugby team in Super Rugby since 1996 and over those 30 years, have built a strong identity and fanbase across New Zealand, Australia and internationally.  

"In New Zealand, NZR owns both the trademark rights for the word Chiefs and the Chiefs logo and since 1998, NZR has also held trademark protection for the Chiefs logo in Australia."

NZR claims it had tried to engage with the ARLC in an attempt to find a resolution, yet the commission was now intent on proceeding with the official launch of the PNG Chiefs on Oct. 21.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said. "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand.   

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."  

The Chiefs won two Super Rugby titles in back-to-back seasons in 2012 and 2013, and were runners-up in Super Rugby Pacific this season after suffering a crushing defeat by the Hurricanes in the decider.

The Hamilton-based team has produced countless All Blacks since its inception, with Saturday's run-on team to face the Wallabies featuring six players from the franchise.

"Here in New Zealand, when people hear 'the Chiefs', they think of this club and this region. The identity carries significant cultural meaning and connection to the region and its people, we know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said.   

"Teams in different sports and markets can exist alongside one another with the same name, but the issue here is the similarity of our sports competing in the same market, for the same fans, in overlapping windows."  

However, ARLC executive chairman Peter V'Landys later issued a stinging rebuke, insisting he would vigorously defend PNG's right to use the Chiefs as its team name.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval. The NSW Blues had been the Blues for in excess of 50 years before that," he said.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

No date has yet been slated for the hearing in New Zealand's High Court.
